title: Été, fête, petit
intro: French has three *e* sounds, and the spelling usually tells you which one: **é** /e/ (*été*), **è** /ɛ/ (*fête*) and **e** /ə/ (*petit*), which often disappears. Hearing the difference really matters: *je mange* (present) and *j'ai mangé* (past) differ only by these sounds!

cases.label: é /e/: été, parler
cases.rule: /e/ is a closed, smiling sound, like *ay* in *say* but without the glide. Spellings: **é** (*été*), **-er, -ez** at the end (*parler, parlez*), **et**, **les, des, mes, ces**, and **ai** in *j'ai*.

cases.label: è /ɛ/: mère, fête, mais
cases.rule: /ɛ/ is more open, like *e* in *bed*. Spellings: **è, ê** (*mère, fête*), **ai, ei** (*mais, neige*), **-et** at the end (*bonnet*), and **e** before two consonants (*belle, merci*).

cases.label: e /ə/: le, petit
cases.rule: /ə/ is short and relaxed, like *a* in *about*: *le, je, de, ce, petit, demain*. It's an **e** with no accent at the end of a syllable.

cases.label: the e that disappears
cases.rule: In everyday speech, /ə/ often drops out: *samedi* /sam.di/, *maintenant* /mɛ̃t.nɑ̃/, *je ne sais pas* → /ʃɛ.pa/.

cases.label: silent -e, -es, -ent
cases.rule: At the end of a word, **-e, -es** and the verb ending **-ent** are silent: *une table, des tables, ils parlent*. But the consonant before the **-e** is heard: *petit* /pə.ti/, *petite* /pə.tit/.

cases.label: le / les, ce / ces
cases.rule: /ə/ or /e/ can be the only difference between singular and plural: *le train / les trains*, *ce quartier / ces quartiers*, *de / des*. Listen carefully!

cases.label: je mange / j'ai mangé
cases.rule: The present and the passé composé often differ only by these vowels: *je mange* /ʒə.mɑ̃ʒ/ (I eat) but *j'ai mangé* /ʒe.mɑ̃.ʒe/ (I ate).

cases.label: -er, -ez, -é: one sound
cases.rule: *parler, vous parlez, j'ai parlé* all end with the same sound: /e/. Only the grammar tells you the spelling.

sections.title: 1. é /e/
text: Smile a little and keep your tongue high: /e/. No glide at the end, unlike English *say*.

examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.

sections.title: 2. è /ɛ/
text: Open your mouth a bit more: /ɛ/, like *e* in *bed*.

examples.en: My mother is getting the party ready.

sections.title: 3. e /ə/
text: Relax your mouth and round your lips slightly: /ə/. It's the sound in **le, je, de, ce, me, ne**, and in many words like *petit, demain, premier*.

sections.title: 4. The e that disappears
text: In everyday speech, French drops many /ə/ sounds. You'll hear the short version all the time, so learn to recognise it.

sections.title: 5. Silent -e, -es, -ent
text: A final **-e** is silent, but it makes the consonant before it heard. That's how you hear the feminine of many adjectives.

sections.title: 6. le / les, ce / ces
text: The plural *-s* is silent, so the article does all the work: /ə/ for one, /e/ for several.

examples.en: The train is leaving. The trains are leaving.

sections.title: 7. je mange / j'ai mangé
text: Listen for /ʒə/ or /ʒe/ at the start and /e/ at the end. That's often the only difference between *now* and *the past*.

examples.en: I'm visiting Montréal. Yesterday, I visited Quebec City.

sections.title: 8. -er, -ez, -é: one sound
sections.tip: Not sure how to spell /e/ at the end of a verb? After *vous*: **-ez**. After another verb or a preposition: **-er** (*je vais manger*). After *avoir*: **-é** (*j'ai mangé*).

mistakes.why: That would be *je mange*, the present.

story.title: Le premier été de Lou
story.en: Lou discovers Montréal. Listen for é, è and e.

lines.fr: C'est {l'été|es-e}. Lou a deux ans, et c'est son premier grand [voyage|voyage].
lines.en: It's summer. Lou is two, and it's her first big trip.

lines.fr: Elle découvre Montréal avec sa {mère|es-è}, son {père|es-è} et sa grande sœur Léa.
lines.en: She's discovering Montréal with her mother, her father and her big sister Léa.

lines.fr: {Le matin|es-schwa}, Lou {mange|es-pc} des céréales. Et toute la journée, elle répète : « {J'ai mangé|es-pc} ! {J'ai mangé|es-pc} ! »
lines.en: In the morning, Lou eats cereal. And all day long, she repeats: “I ate! I ate!”

lines.fr: {Samedi|es-drop}, il y a une {fête|es-è} dans {le quartier|es-le-les} : de la musique, des crêpes, des jeux…
lines.en: On Saturday, there's a party in the neighbourhood: music, crêpes, games…

lines.fr: Lou danse avec {les enfants|es-le-les}. Elle est {petite|es-final}, mais elle danse très bien !
lines.en: Lou dances with the children. She's little, but she dances very well!

lines.fr: « Tu veux encore {danser|es-er-ez} ? » demande Léa. « Oui ! Et toi, tu {as dansé|es-er-ez} ? »
lines.en: “Do you want to dance some more?” asks Léa. “Yes! And you, have you danced?”

lines.fr: Le soir, Lou est fatiguée. Elle regarde le ciel : « Léa, {je ne sais pas|es-drop}… Les étoiles, elles dorment {le|es-schwa} jour ? »
lines.en: In the evening, Lou is tired. She looks at the sky: “Léa, I don't know… Do the stars sleep in the daytime?”

lines.fr: Léa rit : « Oui, ma puce. Et {maintenant|es-drop}, toi aussi, tu vas dormir ! »
lines.en: Léa laughs: “Yes, sweetie. And now it's your turn to sleep!”
